title: The Interview Question That Costs You The Job | Why Do You Want To Work Here
description:
The Interview Question That Costs You The Job | Why Do You Want To Work Here


"Why do you want to work here?" is the interview question that decides if you get the offer, and 99% of candidates give the same rehearsed answer. I spoke to 320 hiring managers about this exact question, and what they actually look for isn't the stock price, the CEO podcast, or the recent acquisition. This video shows you how to answer why do you want to work here in a way that actually builds trust, plus the 2 answers that work and the 3 that quietly kill your chances.


What you'll learn in this video:
- What 320 hiring managers said actually decides "why do you want to work here"
- Why cultural fit really comes down to trust, and how to break the distrust
- The networking name-drop answer that shifts you from candidate to colleague
- The authentic personal story answer, and exactly when to use it
- The 3 answers that quietly kill your chances, and why they fall flat

0:18 What 320 hiring managers actually look for
0:26 Why cultural fit comes down to trust

2:33 The second answer: authentic personal story

5:43 What to do today


If you want the scripts that generate the conversations you can name-drop in any interview, here's how I can help:

I dropped out of university at 19 to build recruitment software and ATS systems used by hiring teams. Today I help job seekers land offers faster using a proven 3-step system. I've coached hundreds of candidates into roles at firms like JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, EY, and PwC and many more.

transcript: So, the why this company answer is the one that decides if you get the offer, and 99% of candidates answer it completely wrong. And there's a reason why cultural fit is the deciding factor is that every candidate gives the same rehearsed version of this answer. So, the employer can't really tell if you're just being authentic. So, they just default to like, "I don't trust this person enough to really bet on them." And you don't get the job offer. So, the only way to break that distrust is to sound like a colleague, not like a candidate. And the strongest way to do that is to name-drop somebody you've actually spoken to at the company before you applied. And I mean like actually spoken to. I don't mean somebody that you found on LinkedIn in 10 minutes ago, and then you just never messaged them. I mean somebody you genuinely had a conversation with before you applied. So, it sounds like this, "I'm applying because I spoke to Sarah who's on your team. She told me about how the work actually gets done day-to-day, and that's the kind of environment that I want to be in." That's the whole answer. It's three sentences long. So, that answer, it does three things. The first thing is that it proves you researched specifically by talking to a human, not just by reading the website. The second is that it builds trust because somebody at the firm already knows who you are. And then the third is that it shifts you from a candidate to being a colleague already in the network. You just haven't really been hired yet. So, this is the answer hiring managers tell me they wish they heard more often. Because the moment that you name a real person, the tone of the interview changes. Now, you're the person Sarah from the team recommended chatting to, not CV number 47, "Oh, we're going to have to work through them this afternoon." So, the mistake people make is that they just hear name-drop, and then they don't have a name. So, what they do is they bail, and they go back to the generic answer. And the fix is to network before you apply, not after. So, what you do is you spend 2 to 3 weeks before your application, sending cold outreach messages to people at your target firms. The job of those messages isn't to land an offer. The job is to land a conversation where you can ask the person what their role is actually like. And then three things happen when you do this. The first is that you learn something specific you would never know from the website. You also can name them in the interview. And then the third is that they sometimes refer you internally without you even asking. So one outreach can produce both the answer to this question and the referral that you got by in the interview in the first place. And there's a second answer that also breaks that distrust. So it's an authentic personal story. So this is the one to use when you genuinely have a personal connection to the company that's not about money or a career progression. So let me give you like an an Apple example. So if you were applying to Apple and you actually love Apple, you wouldn't say I admire your design philosophy. That's everybody's answer. You'd say something like, "I bought my first iPod when I was 14 and I still remember the colors from the campaign XYZ. I've been obsessed with the how Apple makes you feel ever since." It's specific, it's lived, and it's real. And that type of answer signals authenticity because it doesn't sound rehearsed. It sounds like a moment from your life that you remember and you're telling an authentic story. And that means that it can't be copied and pasted from another candidate. And the trust the interviewer was missing, they get it from the way you tell that story. And the trick to this answer is that the story has to be real. So if you don't have one, just don't fake it because the moment a personal story just sounds invented, you've signaled the opposite of authenticity. So if you don't have the story, go back to the first approach and find someone who to network with. So what if you're like interviewing in four days time, you don't have a name, and you don't have an authentic story? So being really honest, this interview is going to be harder than it should have been. But you can still close some of the gaps. So spend an hour finding one concrete thing about the company that you have a genuine view on. Not generic stuff like I admire your culture or I love what you do. Something you've actually thought about where you can defend the view if the interviewer pushes back on it. And then promise yourself that you'll network properly before the next application. Because the most expensive lesson in job searching is realizing the difference between an offer and a rejection. It was a 30-minute conversation that you just didn't have. So, let me give you like three wrong answers I see candidates lean on constantly. So, these are the ones that the 320 hiring managers that I spoke to said either just signal nothing or actively reduce trust. So, mistake number one is commercial awareness. Things like, "Oh, I noticed your stock price hit a record high. I saw that you, you know, had your best quarter." Hiring managers don't care about you read a headline. Anyone can read a headline. The second mistake is then leading with current events. "Oh, I read about your recent acquisition." or "I saw the news about your new product." Same problem. Reading the news isn't research because reading the news takes 4 minutes and the interviewer knows it. Then the final mistake is then quoting like some C-suite executive at a company. "Oh, I watched your CEO on a podcast and liked how he said this." This one feels smart because it sounds specific, but it doesn't really build trust. The CEO is the most public person at the company. Quoting them is just the easiest research move there is. Which means that everyone else can make it. And once everyone else is doing it, it stops signaling the effort. And the pattern across all three wrong answers are the same. Anything that comes from a public source is going to land flat. Trust gets built when you reference something only an insider would know. That's why the networking answer wins. So, if you want the full system for landing offers, the cold outreach scripts that actually generate conversations that you need to name drop in those interviews, and also the networking approach that gets you a referral, and the framework for behavioral questions, and how to build your story bank to questions like, "Why this company?" and "Tell me about yourself." That's all inside the Offer Accelerator. And the link is in the description if you want to check it out. So, the most important thing you can do today is pick the next company you're interviewing. Find three people who work there on LinkedIn and send them a message asking for a conversation. One name in your back pocket is the difference between getting the next round and getting that rejection email.
